description: Solo participant building an interactive space mission design game where players balance power, mass, budget, and communications to design a successful mission. Background in app development (Flutter/Kodular) and Python."
summary:
Apogee Mission Designer is an interactive, browser-based space systems engineering game where students plan, build, budget, and fly deep-space missions to the Moon or Mars. Players choose a destination, a launch vehicle, spacecraft power systems, telecommunications, scientific instruments, and radiation shielding. 

A dynamic simulation engine then evaluates their design across funding approval, launch payload limits, cruise power balance, orbit insertion, and science return. The game reveals the exact trade-offs that constrain space exploration—demonstrating how solar irradiance drops with distance, how data rates decay over interplanetary distances, why the 14-day lunar night challenges surface landers, and why every kilogram of science payload demands strict mass and budget margins.
details:
What it does:

Apogee Mission Designer addresses the "Space Mission Design Game" challenge by turning complex aerospace trade-offs into an intuitive, accessible web simulation that runs seamlessly on phones, tablets, and desktops with zero installation required. Players select from four mission architectures (Moon Orbiter, Moon Lander, Mars Orbiter, Mars Lander), each constrained by strict NASA-style cost caps. Players select a launch vehicle that dictates maximum payload mass and launch reliability, then configure power generation (solar arrays, battery packs, radioisotope thermoelectric generators), antenna gain, scientific payload suites (cameras, spectrometers, radar sounders, environmental stations, seismometers, drills), and radiation shielding.

How it works:

A live Mission Dashboard continuously computes:

- Wet mass against rocket trans-trajectory injection limits.

- Project cost against mission budget caps.

- Solar generation vs. spacecraft electrical draw (accounting for Mars receiving less than half of Earth's solar irradiance).

- Downlink data bandwidth vs. instrument generation rates.

- Battery capacity vs. eclipse and night durations (accounting for the 14-Earth-day lunar night).

When launched, the simulation progresses through five phases: Funding Review, Ascent, Cruise, Arrival, and Science Operations. Surviving missions receive a performance score, a grade benchmarked against an optimal reference architecture, and specific systems engineering debrief notes detailing what bottlenecked their return.

Tools & Technologies:

Built with clean, self-contained HTML5, CSS3, and modern JavaScript, with zero external runtime dependencies. Hosted on Vercel and version-controlled via GitHub under an open-source MIT license.
